newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - AON. ACORDIA.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - AON. ACORDIA.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

Aon chiefs are reeling after being stung for $27 million from investment losses it did not foresee in its acquisition of Alexander & Alexander. The story will amuse rivals and give 'I told you so' satisfaction to those who warned that consolidation in the broking sector was going on too fast without enough time to take stock.
Aon is now considering legal action, but that won't make up for the embarrassment of having to report a second quarter drop in profits despite an increase in revenue.

The chaos consolidation can bring is well illustrated by the practical tasks reorganisation has presented to Aon in the UK. In the last year Aon has bought Bain Hogg, Alexander & Alexander and its subsidiaries and Minet. Previously Nicholson Leslie was acquired by Aon-owned Rollins Hudig Hall, itself an amalgamation of three companies.

As a result Aon is now trying to move staff, equipment and records from 10 or 11 UK offices into just three. The task involves a move taking place every weekend for the next two months, and every office is awash with packing crates.

Stateside the world's seventh largest broker, Acordia, has come into the hands of a group of investors for the bargain price of $320 million. It never had any intention of being sold to a rival broker and therefore avoided the agonies of merger.

The new Acordia will remain a holding company, but rather than having 35 Acordia companies, the broker has seven regional operations plus a stand-alone, multi-state excess and surplus lines operation, American E&S Insurance Brokers. While Acordia is only half its previous size, its predominately property/ casualty brokerage business remains very much the same.
Its main problem is international expansion, and questions will be asked as to whether the new parents will be willing to bankroll this.
In 1996, only two percent of gross revenues was generated by non-U.S. clients, and company chiefs have in the past talked up the idea of an acquisition to redress the situation.

One less expensive option may be strategic alliances. Acordia was well on its way to increasing its international exposure with the 1995 formation of ExcelNet, a reciprocal arrangement among Acordia, Dale-Parizeau of Montreal, CECAR of Paris, Bain Hogg Group of London, Inchcape Insurance Services of Hong Kong and Boels & Begault of Brussels, Belgium.
The network, however, fell victim to brokerage consolidation in 1996 and 1997 when Bain Hogg, Boels & Begault and Dale-Parizeau sold to Aon Group, and CECAR sold to Marsh & McLennan.
No doubt there are several European broker firms who would consider themselves ideal candidates.
